title: The Mississippi vs Latin America: A River Map and a $72,000 Gap

thumbnail.idea: Full-frame relief map of the Americas: the Mississippi basin glowing green with its blue river network converging on one bold arrow at New Orleans, which is circled; Latin America in brown relief with the Andes ridge and Amazon forest shaded dark, no rivers lit.

minor: Serra do Mar line: 'every load of coffee, and later soy, had to cross' overstates it. The script itself says soy now also goes north via the Tapajós, and Paranaguá is reached by another route. Use 'most coffee, and much of the soy'.

Panama Canal: daily transits were cut stepwise from about 36 through late 2023 into early 2024 (about 24 around the turn of the year, then lower). 'In late 2023 ... to about 24' is close, but 'by the turn of 2024' is safer.
Gran Colombia 'formed in 1819' with today's Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador and Panama: Panama (1821) and Ecuador (1822) joined after the 1819 founding. Wording could be 'by 1822 included'.

Gallup, Sachs and Mellinger line: the 'even after controlling for institutions' claim fits Sachs's 2003 follow-up better than the 1999 paper, and the line gives no year. The line is attributed, but add the paper and year.
Argentine dredging: 'has been trying to award a new one since' needs a status check against the latest tender news before publishing, given the sources are 2021 and 2025.

'Ocean ships sail about 230 river miles up from the mouth': the Corps figure is measured from Head of Passes, not the Gulf bar, so the real distance from the sea is a little more. Say 'about 230 river miles above Head of Passes'.
The (quote) shot on the Nobel line contains no quotation. Either use the Academy's wording ('for studies of how institutions are formed and affect prosperity') or retag it as a document or headline.
'Months earlier, Jefferson had written': the letter is 18 April 1802, about six months before the October closure. This is accurate, but name the month.

shots.vo: The Mississippi river system drains 41 percent of the lower 48 states.
Its barges carry Midwest grain to one exit: New Orleans.
Jefferson named New Orleans the one spot whose owner was America's enemy.

document.title: Thomas Jefferson to Robert R. Livingston, 18 April 1802
document.highlight: There is on the globe one single spot, the possessor of which is our natural and habitual enemy. It is New Orleans.

shots.vo: The US makes 82,800 a person; Latin America and the Caribbean, just over 10,000.
That is a gap of about 72,000 dollars for every person.

stat.label: Gap in GDP per person, US vs Latin America, 2023 (World Bank)

shots.vo: When that river runs low, barge rates spike.
So did a river decide who got rich, or did people?
In 1700, Mexico was richer than British North America.
The basin covers about 1.2 million square miles, from the Rockies to the Appalachians, draining 31 states.
Two Canadian provinces drain into it too, and the National Park Service ranks it the fourth largest watershed on Earth.
Barges can work the main stem for about 1,800 river miles, from Minneapolis all the way down to the Gulf of Mexico.
The Ohio adds 981 more miles, starting at Pittsburgh, where the coal and steel of the old industrial east were loaded.
The Missouri adds a 735-mile channel from Sioux City, Iowa, reaching west into the farm country of the Plains.
Between those rivers lies the Corn Belt, and by USDA figures the United States is the world's largest corn producer.
The land is so low that St. Louis, over 1,000 river miles from the sea, stands less than 150 metres above it.
On water this flat, one gallon of fuel moves a ton of cargo 647 miles by barge, and only 145 by truck.
One standard tow of 15 barges carries what it would take about 1,050 semi trucks to haul by road.
In all, the Army Corps of Engineers maintains about 12,000 miles of commercial inland waterways across the country.
The Mississippi, Ohio and Missouri routes alone, about 3,500 miles, all lead to the lower river between Baton Rouge and the Gulf.
Ocean ships sail about 230 river miles up from the mouth to Baton Rouge, where barges hand cargo straight to them.
About six in ten American grain exports leave through these Gulf ports, according to the US Agriculture Department.
The forecasting firm Stratfor wrote in 2011 that this basin had more navigable river than the rest of the world combined.
China's own statistics disagree: its transport ministry counts about 128,000 kilometres of navigable inland waterways at home.
Definitions differ, but what is rare is the shape: one connected tree of rivers, under one flag, emptying through a single door.
Now look south, where one continent holds the largest river on Earth and a second basin almost the Mississippi's size.
The Amazon carries about one fifth of all the fresh water that rivers pour into the oceans, Britannica estimates.

map.label: ≈1/5 of river water to the sea

shots.vo: Ocean ships can sail about 3,700 kilometres up it to Iquitos, Peru, a city with no road link to Lima.
But it runs through rainforest and flooded lowland, far from the coasts and highlands where most South Americans have always lived.

map.label: Forest inland, people on the edges

shots.vo: The closer match is the Río de la Plata basin: about 3.1 million square kilometres of plains, swamps and rivers.
But its rivers cross five countries, Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay and Bolivia, before they ever reach the sea.
Elsewhere the great cities sit high, with Mexico City at 2,240 metres, Bogotá at 2,640 and Quito at 2,850.
Brazil's largest city, São Paulo, stands about 760 metres up, only 65 kilometres from its port at Santos.
Between them rises the Serra do Mar, a coastal wall that every load of coffee, and later soy, had to cross.

shots.vo: So the north got one funnel, and the south got mountains, forests and borders. Yet in 1700, none of it seemed to matter.
By Angus Maddison's estimates, in 1990 dollars, Mexico produced about 568 dollars per person in 1700, against 527 in the colonies that became the US.
Spain's wealth was not in river valleys but in silver, much of it from Potosí, over 4,000 metres up in the Andes.
Mule trains carried that silver down to the Pacific at Arica, then ships took it north to Callao, the port of Lima.
From there it sailed to Panama, crossed the isthmus overland to Portobelo, and was loaded onto the fleets bound for Spain.
By law the fleets answered to one office in Seville, the Casa de Contratación, which Spain set up in 1503.
Buenos Aires, at the mouth of the south's great river system, was kept off the legal trade routes for most of the colonial era.
Only in 1776 did Spain make Buenos Aires a viceroyalty's capital, and only in 1778 did it loosen the rules on trade.

timeline.title: Spain's southern door
events: Viceroyalty of Río de la Plata

shots.vo: The line drawn: in Spanish America, the roads ran from mines in the mountains to a few licensed ports, not along the rivers.
In the north, the British colonies hugged the Atlantic coast, and the Appalachians stood between them and the interior.
When American settlers crossed into the Ohio Valley, the only cheap way to sell their crops was downriver to New Orleans.
And New Orleans was Spanish: in 1795 the Pinckney Treaty gave Americans the right to ship through it and store goods there.
In 1800 Spain secretly agreed to pass Louisiana back to France, and in October 1802 its officials closed the port's warehouses to Americans.

headline.text: Spain suspends Americans' right to store goods at New Orleans

shots.vo: Months earlier, Jefferson had written that three-eighths of American territory had to send its produce to market through that one port.

document.title: Thomas Jefferson to Robert R. Livingston, 18 April 1802
document.highlight: It is New Orleans, through which the produce of three-eighths of our territory must pass to market.

shots.vo: In 1803 the United States bought Louisiana from France for 15 million dollars, about 828,000 square miles of land.
The country roughly doubled in size, and New Orleans, at the river's mouth, now answered to one government.
In 1811 the first steamboat on these rivers left Pittsburgh for New Orleans, and steam power began to make upstream trips possible.
In 1825 the Erie Canal linked the Great Lakes to New York, and in 1848 another canal joined Lake Michigan to the Mississippi system.
By Maddison's estimates the order had flipped by 1820: about 1,257 dollars per person in the US, against 759 in Mexico.
Economic historians treat those figures as rough, but the line drawn is clear: one basin, one market, and a door the country owned.
Spanish America won its independence between 1810 and the mid-1820s, but the empire's pieces did not stay together.
Gran Colombia, formed in 1819, put today's Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador and Panama under a single government in Bogotá.
It broke apart in 1831, after barely a decade, into Venezuela, Ecuador and New Granada, which included Panama.
The Federal Republic of Central America lasted from 1823 to 1841 before it split into five separate states.
And the Plata basin, the south's one great river funnel, ended up divided between five countries with five capitals.
From 1864 to 1870, Paraguay fought Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay; historians still debate the causes, and river access is among them.
The line drawn: the south's best river map was cut by borders, and each stretch of water answered to a different capital.
Yet by 1913, on Maddison's estimates, Argentina, sitting on that very basin, had pulled far ahead of Mexico, at 3,797 dollars per person.

chart.title: Argentina's river boom
chart.source: Maddison, The World Economy: A Millennial Perspective, OECD, 2001

shots.vo: Which raises the hardest question for the map: if rivers made America rich, why did they not keep Argentina rich?
Two camps answer that question, and both deserve a hearing.
The geography camp, writers like Peter Zeihan in 2014 and Tim Marshall in 2015, argue that cheap transport shaped where wealth gathered.
In that view, a farmer who can ship cheaply keeps more of each harvest, and the surplus builds banks, towns and factories.
The institutions camp won the economics Nobel in 2024: Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson and James Robinson.

quote.text: for studies of how institutions are formed and affect prosperity
quote.who: Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, on Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson

shots.vo: Acemoglu and Robinson's book Why Nations Fail opens in Nogales, a city split in two by the US-Mexico border.
Same land and same climate on both sides of the fence, so the income gap, they argue, comes from the rules each side lives under.
In a 2002 paper, the three argued that the colonies richest around 1500 tend to be the poorer ones today.
Where Spain found silver and dense populations to tax, they argue, it built rules to extract wealth rather than spread it.
In 1997, economists Stanley Engerman and Kenneth Sokoloff argued that soils and crops did shape the Americas, through inequality.
Sugar and plantation colonies, they wrote, put land in few hands, while wheat-farm colonies spread it among many families.
Which do you find more convincing, the river or the rules?
To the institutions camp, Argentina is a case in point: it had the Plata's rivers and plains, and still fell behind across the twentieth century.

Geography writers Gallup, Sachs and Mellinger argue that coastal and navigable-river economies are richer worldwide, even after controlling for institutions, though the institutions camp disputes this.
The rivalry is not only academic; it runs straight through the world's soybean trade today.
By USDA figures, Brazil is now the world's largest soybean exporter, competing head-on with the American Midwest for buyers.
But Brazil's soy belt sits deep inland, and from Sorriso in Mato Grosso, trucks drive about 2,000 kilometres to Santos.
So soy has been pushed north as well, by truck to Amazon tributaries like the Tapajós, then by barge to ports near the river's mouth.
Paraguay, with no coast at all, ships its grain down the Paraguay and Paraná rivers, and its shipowners say it runs the world's third largest barge fleet.
That route, the Paraná-Paraguay waterway, runs about 3,442 kilometres, from Cáceres in Brazil down to Nueva Palmira in Uruguay.
It is the south's nearest thing to a Mississippi, but its channel answers to several governments, not one.
And in November 2024 a new deep-water port opened at Chancay, north of Lima, majority owned by China's state shipping group COSCO.

headline.text: Chinese-majority megaport opens at Chancay, north of Lima

shots.vo: COSCO holds 60 percent and the Peruvian miner Volcan 40, and the first phase cost about 1.3 billion dollars.
Peru's government calls it a hub for the whole region, while US officials have said they worry about Chinese control of strategic ports.
For the US, the question is whether its great funnel keeps its edge, and the river itself has been showing strain.
In October 2022 the Mississippi hit a record low at Memphis, and barges carried lighter loads to avoid running aground.

headline.text: Mississippi falls to record low at Memphis; barges lighten loads

shots.vo: That month the USDA's weekly barge report showed record spot rates for barges loading at St. Louis.
Upstream, the Upper Mississippi's 29 locks and dams were mostly built in the 1930s, and many are past their 50-year design life.
In its 2021 report card, the American Society of Civil Engineers gave the nation's inland waterways a grade of D-plus.

document.title: ASCE 2021 Report Card for America's Infrastructure: Inland Waterways

shots.vo: If a major lock failed, cargo above it would have to move by rail and road instead, at a higher fuel cost per ton.
Engineers have long warned of a bigger risk at Old River, Louisiana, where the Mississippi tends to shift into the shorter, steeper Atchafalaya.
The Atchafalaya reaches the Gulf in about 140 miles, against roughly 300 on the Mississippi's present path, John McPhee wrote.
Since 1963 the Army Corps has held it in place with the Old River Control Structure, letting about 30 percent of the flow go west.
If the river ever broke through, McPhee wrote, Baton Rouge and New Orleans could be left on a saltwater channel.
In the south, the Paraná's private dredging concession, held since 1995, expired in 2021, and Argentina has been trying to award a new one since.
If the waterway were deepened and run as one system, the Plata could carry far more grain to sea, with Rosario as its New Orleans.
The region's one great water shortcut, the Panama Canal, depends on rain, and in late 2023 drought cut daily transits to about 24, from roughly 36.
Some shippers and officials have pointed to routes that avoid it, like Chancay to the west, Reuters reported in 2024.
And Mexico, with almost no navigable rivers, became America's largest trading partner in 2023, with about 798 billion dollars in goods.
That trade moves by rail and truck through crossings like Laredo, a line on the map that runs north to south, not down a river.
If that keeps growing, the line that matters most in the Americas may no longer be one that water drew.
Whichever camp is right, the map helped set the price of moving a harvest, and the north's rivers gave it unusually cheap transport, by the figures above.

map.label: The price of moving a harvest

shots.vo: Next, the Strait of Malacca, and how the city at its tip came to out-earn the country that founded it.
